passage: The courtyard in their village near Jorhat was full of relatives and the smell of incense when Aita's body was carried out. Alka, ten, sat on the steps with dry eyes. Everyone else was crying. She tugged her father's sleeve. 'Deuta, can I have some pitha? I'm hungry.' Bhupen stared at her, then nodded slowly and fetched a plate. Later she asked if she could watch cartoons on Mami's phone. A cousin whispered that Alka didn't even care. But when the cartoon ended, Alka didn't ask for another. She sat very still, holding the phone, looking at Aita's empty chair by the door, and didn't say a word until dark.

qa.q: What did Alka ask her father for?
qa.a: She asked for some pitha because she was hungry.

qa.q: Why might Alka seem so calm and ask for food and cartoons?
qa.a: The loss may be too big to take in at once, so her mind is keeping it at a distance; it doesn't mean she doesn't care.

qa.q: How could Bhupen support Alka at this stage?
qa.a: He could let her eat and rest without judging, stay near her, and gently tell her she can talk or cry whenever she's ready.

qa.q: Why is the cousin's whisper that Alka 'didn't even care' unfair?
qa.a: The cousin sees only her calm surface, not the stillness and silence by Aita's chair that suggest deep feeling held back.

grounding: After her grandmother's death a ten-year-old seems oddly calm, asks for food and cartoons, then falls silent as the feeling is held at a distance.

passage: The call from Enugu came on Saturday morning: Chidi's grandpa had died in the night. Mum cried in the kitchen of their Houston apartment. Chidi, nine, sat at the counter and asked, 'Can I still have pancakes?' Dad made them, slowly. When Jin knocked to ask if Chidi could play video games, Chidi said yes and played for an hour, laughing at the usual jokes. Jin didn't know yet. After Jin left, Chidi switched off the screen and sat on the sofa with Grandpa's last birthday card in his lap. He didn't open it. He didn't cry. He just stayed there, very quiet, until the light outside turned orange.

qa.q: Where did the call about Chidi's grandpa come from?
qa.a: The call came from Enugu.

qa.q: What might Chidi's playing and laughing, then sitting silently with the card, suggest?
qa.a: The loss seems too big to feel all at once; he held it at a distance while playing, and it began to come closer when he was alone.

qa.q: What might help Chidi now, as he sits quietly with the card?
qa.a: A parent sitting beside him without pushing, maybe saying 'We can open it together whenever you want,' so he knows he isn't alone with it.

qa.q: What might Jin feel on learning later what had happened that morning?
qa.a: Jin may be surprised Chidi seemed so normal, and perhaps unsure about having joked around, then glad to have kept him company.

grounding: A nine-year-old asks for pancakes and plays games after his grandfather's death, then goes quiet, as the loss is too big to feel at once.

passage:
Dear diary,
Nani died on Thursday. Everyone was crying at the house. I wasn't. I asked Mumma if I could have noodles and watch cartoons. Some aunties looked at me funny.
My cousin Divyansh said, "Don't you even care?"
I do care. I just couldn't feel anything. It was like my feelings were in another room.
Then at night I was lying in bed and I didn't want to talk to anyone. I just looked at the fan going round and round. I still can't cry. Is that bad?
Arohi

qa.q: What did Arohi ask Mumma for?
qa.a: Noodles, and to watch cartoons.

qa.q: How did Arohi describe the feeling of not crying?
qa.a: Arohi felt numb and confused, as if the feelings were in another room, and worried about not crying.

qa.q: How could a grown-up gently help Arohi now?
qa.a: Tell Arohi it is okay not to cry yet, stay nearby, and let feelings come in their own time.

qa.q: What might Divyansh have been thinking when asking "Don't you even care?"
qa.a: Divyansh may have been upset and confused, not understanding that numbness can be part of grief.

grounding: Shows a child who, after a grandparent's death, seems calm, asks for food and cartoons, then goes quiet because the feeling is too big.

passage:
The house in the village was full of relatives from Rampur. Men sat on the charpais outside; women cooked in the courtyard. Yusuf's Nana had died that morning.
Yusuf sat in the corner, dry-eyed. When Rekha aunty from next door brought a plate of rice, he ate every bit. "Can I watch the TV?" he asked. His uncle frowned.
Rekha aunty put a hand on the uncle's arm. "Let him."
Yusuf watched cartoons with the sound low. He didn't laugh. After a while he turned it off and sat very still, looking at Nana's slippers by the door. He didn't say anything for the rest of the evening.

qa.q: What did Rekha aunty bring Yusuf?
qa.a: A plate of rice.

qa.q: What does Yusuf staring at Nana's slippers suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He seems numb and far away, the grief too big to take in yet, even though he is quiet and dry-eyed.

qa.q: What did Rekha aunty do that helped?
qa.a: She stopped the uncle from scolding and let Yusuf watch cartoons, accepting his calm as a way of coping.

qa.q: How might Yusuf's uncle see his behaviour?
qa.a: His uncle may feel disapproving or confused, thinking Yusuf should be crying instead of asking for TV.

grounding: Shows a child in a village who, after his grandfather's death, calmly eats and asks for cartoons, then goes quiet and still.

passage:
In Berlin, Elif's Babaanne died on a Tuesday. Her parents flew to Istanbul for the funeral, and Elif stayed with the neighbours.
Tuan, the boy next door, didn't know what to say. But Elif seemed fine. She asked his mum for pasta. She asked if they could watch the robot cartoon. She even laughed at it.
Then, halfway through, Elif went quiet. She pulled her knees up and stared at the screen without watching it. When Tuan asked if she wanted juice, she didn't answer.
Tuan's mum sat down beside her on the sofa, not asking anything, and just stayed.

qa.q: Where did Elif's parents fly for the funeral?
qa.a: To Istanbul.

qa.q: What was Elif feeling when she pulled her knees up and stared?
qa.a: She seemed numb and far away, her grief too big to take in, after seeming fine a moment before.

qa.q: What did Tuan's mum do that helped?
qa.a: She sat beside Elif quietly without asking questions, letting her be numb or sad as she needed.

qa.q: How might Tuan be experiencing Elif's change?
qa.a: Tuan seems confused and unsure, not knowing what to say when Elif suddenly goes silent.

grounding: Shows a child who seems calm after her grandmother's death, asking for food and cartoons, then suddenly goes quiet.

passage: In the family room at the end of the hospital corridor, the adults were crying quietly and making phone calls. Salma sat on a plastic chair, swinging her legs. Dadu had died an hour ago. "Can I have the orange biscuits from the machine?" she asked. Phuppo stared at her, then found some coins. Salma ate three biscuits and asked if she could watch cartoons on Phuppo's phone. The ward attendant who brought tea smiled at her gently and said nothing about it. The cartoon played. Halfway through, Salma stopped watching. She held the phone in her lap, looking at the door of Dadu's room, and didn't speak for a long time. When her mother sat down beside her, Salma leaned in without a word.

qa.q: What did Salma ask for from the machine?
qa.a: She asked for the orange biscuits from the machine.

qa.q: Why might Salma seem so calm at first in the family room?
qa.a: The loss may be too big to take in yet, so she keeps it at a distance with biscuits and cartoons before going quiet and sad.

qa.q: How could an adult support Salma now?
qa.a: Sitting close as her mother does, answering questions simply and not scolding her calm lets her feel it at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Phuppo see Salma's request for biscuits?
qa.a: Phuppo, who stares at first, might find it strange or even uncaring before realising that a child takes in a death differently.

grounding: Shows a child who seems oddly calm right after a grandparent's death, asking for snacks and cartoons, then falling quiet.
